Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 90, verses 1–3:

﴿لا أقسم﴾ ... ﴿في كبد﴾

The city refers to Makkah, where the Sacred House (Bayt al-Haram) stands. It is the first house built on this earth exclusively for the worship of Allah, so that people may come to it freely and live in peace. Upon arriving there, they lay down their weapons, set aside their personal disputes, forget their enmities, and gather in complete safety. In it, it is forbidden for anyone to raise a weapon against another human being, and it is also forbidden to disturb or harm its birds and trees. Furthermore, this city is the home of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), the father of Isma'il (peace be upon him), and Isma'il (peace be upon him) is the father of the Arabs and the leader of the Muslims.

Allah honours the Prophet ﷺ in this way: He swears by this city while you (O Prophet) are residing in it. That is, through your presence here, the honour, respect, dignity, greatness and majesty of this city have increased. This allusion carries profound significance at this place, in circumstances where the polytheists were violating the sanctity of this House, and in this city, where even plants and animals were safe, the Muslims were being tormented. Although this House was already sacred, it became even more sacred through the presence of the Noble Prophet ﷺ, and when Allah swore an oath by this city and the personality residing in it, its sanctity, glory and status increased further. Therefore, the claim of the polytheists of Makkah that they are the servants of this House, that they are descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him), and that they follow the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), is entirely false, contradictory and untrue.

This is the reason for the next oath.

﴿ووالد وما ولد﴾ (90:3) "And by the father and what he begot." Here there is a specific allusion to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his son Isma'il (peace be upon him). The oath by Makkah, by the Final Prophet residing in it, and by the founders of Makkah, Ibrahim and Isma'il (peace be upon them), share a relevance. However, despite this allusion and relevance, "the father" and "the begotten" may also mean any father and any offspring in general. In that case, the meaning is that this verse swears by human birth and human growth, and thus this oath serves as a preface to the main theme of the surah, which is the reality of man.

Ustadh Muhammad Abduh has offered a particular interpretation at this point and expressed a subtle insight that is consistent with the spirit of Zilal al-Quran. Therefore, we consider it appropriate to quote it here. He says:

"Then Allah swore by the father and the begotten, because among the phenomena of this universe, the manifestation of the birth and growth of humanity is very significant, namely the system of reproduction and the profound wisdom hidden within it, and how beautifully Allah has created the human being. Furthermore, both the father and the begotten bear great hardship in the perfection of the one being born, and through how many difficulties and efforts this offspring reaches its appointed perfection."

"The same condition occurs in the sprouting and growth of a seed through all its stages. This seed and plant must confront the factors of the environment, and this plant, with effort, draws various elements from its surroundings for itself, until at last it becomes a tree with a trunk and branches. Then this tree and the complete plant produce further seeds, and these seeds in turn play their role, and thus this earth is made beautiful by these plants. If you keep all these matters in mind and then reflect a little higher upon animals, you will find that the wonders in the biology of the father and the begotten are very great, and that the hardships both the father and the begotten undergo in this process of growth, and the way the continuation of the species is arranged through this means, and the way through them the beauty of this universe is enhanced, are in this process among the most elevated and important manifestations of divine power."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 90, verse 4:

And what is the answer to this oath, and for what truth was this oath taken?

﴿Indeed, We have created man in toil.﴾ (90:4) That is, man was created in hardship, in constant struggle, and in a state of confronting difficulties and calamities, as Allah says elsewhere: ﴿O man, indeed you are toiling toward your Lord with exertion, and you will meet Him.﴾ (84:6)

When a cell settles in the womb, from the very first day it begins to strive, to secure its own nourishment and to prepare good conditions for the life ahead. It does all of this in accordance with the guidance of the Lord, the Exalted. Within the womb this struggle continues in this way, until the time comes for it to emerge. Then, like its mother, it bears the pains of labour; it is subjected to intense pressure as it leaves the womb, and when it comes out and sees the light, there is pressure upon it still.

As soon as it comes out, a new struggle begins: when it draws in air and begins the act of breathing, and for the first time opens its mouth, its lungs start working, and it suffers severe pain and begins to cry out. Its blood begins to circulate. Then its digestive system starts to work. All these processes are such that it is not accustomed to them; its intestines are not accustomed to expelling waste. In short, from then on every step it takes is taken with hardship, and every movement is an exertion. Just look: now it is crawling on its knees; then it tries to stand on its feet and walks. All these are hardships, and at every stage there is struggle.

Then, when the teeth come out, there is hardship; in standing upright there is hardship; in walking steadily there is hardship; in acquiring knowledge there is hardship; in reflecting there is hardship. In short, every new experience that he undergoes, just as he underwent the experience of crawling on his knees, is toil and struggle.

Now read further: these hardships then branch out. Look, one toils with his muscles as a labourer. Another toils with his thought; this one is labouring with his soul. Look, one is struggling for a morsel of barley; another is struggling for a second worm; and this one is turning a thousand into two thousand. Then ten thousand and beyond. Look, this one is striving for a government and for rank. Among them, look, one is striving in the way of Allah; some are slaves of pleasures and desires; some are labouring for Hell, while others, in contrast, are striving for Paradise. Every person is carrying his burden and moving forward, drawing near to his Lord with great exertion. And when all stand before Allah on the plain of Resurrection, the wretched will be seized by perpetual toil and calamity, while the righteous and the fortunate will be granted a great blessing and rest.

The truth is that worldly life is indeed a toil, but its forms of toil are varied; despite the difference in their nature, in reality it is the toil of life. But the one who suffers the greatest loss is the person who, after undergoing all the toil and constant hardship of this world, arrives at a most lasting and bitter toil and is cast into Hell. And the most successful in this struggle is the person who, in the most painful manner, moves towards his Lord, and by earning such gains, lifts the burden of this worldly life from his shoulders, and in the end attains lasting success and enduring comfort.

Yes, it is true that sometimes some reward for the hardships of this world is also received in this world, because the one who strives for a lofty purpose is not like the one who labours for some petty matter. One spends his life and wealth for a lofty purpose, and the other for base purposes; the joy, contentment and spiritual delight of the two cannot be equal. The one who labours and strives, and has no material aim before him, or who is striving to escape this materialism, is not like the one who is consumed for that materialism in the way that insects and creeping things toil to fill their bellies. The one who strives for the establishment of the religion is not like the one who dies in pursuit of some worldly desire; the toil and the sense of consciousness of the two are not equal. After clarifying the reality of life, a critical commentary is made on certain notions, concepts, claims and certain conduct of man!

This human being was created in toil, and throughout the whole of this worldly life he cannot be free of that toil. Yet he forgets his own reality. When his Creator grants him strength, power, perception and resources, he deals with these faculties as if he is accountable to no one, expects no reckoning, and fears no mighty and worthy power that could seize him and call him to account. Therefore this person gives, seizes, snatches, plunders, accumulates, increases, and commits wickedness and debauchery, with complete fearlessness and complete boldness. These are the features of a person whose heart is empty of faith.

Then, when on occasions such as those mentioned in this surah he is invited to spend in the way of good, he says:

﴿I have squandered abundant wealth﴾ (6:90). And it is enough for him, in his own estimation, that he has squandered such wealth.

﴿Does he think that ... anyone ...﴾ (7:90). He forgets that Allah is watching. Allah's knowledge encompasses even the matters of hearts. Allah sees everything he has spent, and He knows for what purpose he spent it. But this person forgets this reality too, and thinks that perhaps he is hidden from Allah's sight.

Against this human arrogance and this pretence that he is powerful and mighty, and against his stinginess coupled with his claim of having spent abundantly, the Qur'an holds up the mirror of his own self before him and tells him: just reflect on how much Allah has bestowed mercies upon you within your own self and within your very make-up, and how many capacities He has given you. Yet, O human, you have not even given thanks for a single one of these blessings and capacities.

Man is always proud of his strength, although whatever small strength he has is given to him by Allah. Then man is very stingy with wealth, although this wealth too has been given by Allah. Despite this, he neither takes the path of guidance nor offers thanks to the Bestower (shukr-e-mun'im). Allah gave him the hawas-e-khamsa (the five senses), through which he works in the perceptible world ('alam-e-mahsusat). Then He gave him eyes, and how fine and intricate their structure is, and the means through which he sees things. Then Allah gave him the power of speech, and the organ of speech is also wonderful: the tongue and the two lips.

﴿Did We not make for him ... and the two highways?﴾

"And a tongue and two lips" (9:90). After this, Allah gave man the ability to distinguish between good and evil. He gave him the power of reasoning to differentiate between guidance and misguidance, and between truth and falsehood.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 90, verse 10:

[Qur'an 90:10] "And shown him the two highways" (wa hadaynahu al-najdayn). That is, he is shown the paths of good and evil, so that he may choose whichever path he wills. He was given the capacity to adopt whichever of good and evil he wishes. This dual capacity was placed in the creation of man, and this was the wisdom of Allah in creation. Then Allah gave everything its form of creation and made easy for it, in this universe, the duty assigned to it.

This verse clarifies what the nature of man is, and it is further clarified in Surah al-Shams.

[Qur'an 91:7-10] "And by the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety. He has indeed succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it." In these verses the viewpoint of Islam regarding the self (nafs) is stated. Its details will be explained in Surah al-Shams.

These are the blessings of Allah which He has bestowed upon the children of Adam, and these blessings have been placed in the self of every human being. Their requirement is that man accept guidance. It is the duty of his eyes to observe the proofs of divine power in the universe and to seek the signs of faith, and the proofs of power and the signs of faith are scattered everywhere in this universe. Then man's tongue and his lips are the means of speech and expression, and through these two man does much on this earth. Sometimes a single word works like a sword or a bomb, and sometimes it casts the one who utters it into the fire. In short, it is words that raise man up and cast him down, that is, into that fire.

It is narrated from Hadrat Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey. One day I came close to him and began walking alongside him. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me a deed that will admit me into Paradise and save me from the Fire." He said: "You have asked a great thing, but it is easy for those for whom Allah makes it easy. It is that you worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, establish prayer, pay zakat, fast in Ramadan, and perform Hajj to the House of Allah." Then he said: "Shall I not tell you the gates of good? Fasting is a shield, and charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire, and prayer in the last part of the night is the mark of the righteous." And he recited the verse: [Qur'an 32:16] "Their sides forsake their beds." Then he said: "Shall I not tell you the head of this matter, its pillar, and its highest peak?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "The head of this matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its highest peak is jihad." Then he said: "Shall I not tell you what all of these depend upon?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said, pointing to his tongue: "Restrain this." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be held accountable for what we say?" He said: "May your mother lose you! Do people get thrown on their faces or on their noses into the Fire except for the harvest of their tongues?" (Ahmad, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah)

Then Allah showed man the way: He guided him to distinguish between good and evil, and to understand which path leads to Paradise and which path leads to Hell. In the following verses Allah has also clarified this difficult steep path:

Fa-la-iqtahamal-'aqabah ... al-maymanah

This is the arduous ravine which a person does not dare to cross, unless those who seek help through their firm faith. This ravine stands between man and Paradise; if a person crosses it, he enters Paradise directly. Here the Qur'an depicts it in such a way that a longing to cross it is stirred in the human heart, and an urge is created that he should cross it, make a leap, and get to the other side. It has been fully explained, and the assurance has been given that this is what lies between you and Paradise.

﴿Fa-la-iqtahama al-'aqabah﴾ (90:11) "But he has not attempted the steep ascent." By using the word iqtiham (plunging forward), the call is made to advance, to cross it with a single leap, to plunge in.

Then, to describe the greatness and grandeur of this steep path, the question is posed:

﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ (90:12)

This question is not asked because the path is enormous and impassable; rather, the meaning is that it is very important. In the sight of Allah it must be crossed, so that a person boldly enters it and makes the leap, even though difficulties stand in its way. For no work is accomplished without toil and hardship, and whoever bears this hardship will surely obtain its fruit, the reward of his sufferings will be before him, none of his deeds will be wasted, and this matter is bound to happen in every circumstance.

What is this steep path? It is that which the society of Makkah was in dire need of, where the Islamic movement was carrying out the work of da'wah. Freeing the slaves who were working in the most wretched conditions in that society; in that selfish society people were chasing their interests with extreme selfishness, and the poor were dying of hunger. Providing the basic human necessities to people — these matters belong to the background of Makkan society. The rest are matters that are not tied to any particular time or place, which concern all human beings, and which have always been like a steep path for salvation, for example:

﴿Then he becomes one of those who believe and enjoin one another to patience and enjoin one another to compassion﴾ (90:17)

It is narrated in reports that the purpose of freeing a neck from slavery is to take part in the freeing of slaves. Linguistically, 'itq (عتق) means to grant complete freedom to someone, that is, one person sets another free. Whether someone shares in another's freedom or fully frees someone, the outcome of both is the same.

When these verses were revealed, the people of Makkah had surrounded Islam on every side. There was no Islamic government that could pass a law for the freedom of slaves. Slavery was common in the Arabian Peninsula and throughout the rest of the world, and women across the world were treated with extremely cruel behaviour. When some slaves embraced Islam, such as 'Ammar ibn Yasir, his family, Bilal ibn Rabah, Suhayb (رضي الله عنه) and others, their masters began to inflict severe torture upon them, torture that was unbearable. The Muslims concluded that they could be freed from it only through liberation, and there was only one way to achieve their freedom: to buy them from their merciless and hard-hearted masters. In this field Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) was the first among men, as was his habit: he always responded first to every matter of Islam, and he advanced upon this path with great steadfastness, composure and perseverance.

Ibn Ishaq writes that Hadrat Bilal, the freed slave of Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه), had previously been a hereditary slave of the Banu Jumah. He was a most truthful Muslim and of a most pure heart. Umayyah ibn Khalaf ibn Wahb ibn Hudhafah ibn Jumah would take him out in the scorching midday heat, lay him on his back on the ground in the valley of Makkah, and order that a heavy stone be placed on his chest, saying to him: "You will remain in this state until you die, or you deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza." In that calamitous state he would say only: "Ahad... Ahad."

One day Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) passed by while these people were inflicting torture upon him in this manner. Hadrat Abu Bakr's house was in the Banu Jumah quarter. He said to Umayyah ibn Khalaf: "Do you not fear Allah? How long will you continue this oppression?" He replied: "It is you who have ruined him, so you yourself should rescue him from this punishment." Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) said: "Very well, I will do it. I have a black slave who is stronger and more robust than him, and he follows your religion. I give him to you in exchange for this man." Umayyah ibn Khalaf said: "I accept." So Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) bought him in exchange for his slave and set him free.

Before migrating to Madinah, Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) freed six other slaves in addition to these, Bilal being the seventh. (Among them was) 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah (رضي الله عنه), who took part in Badr and was martyred at Bi'r Ma'unah. Umm 'Ubays and Zunayrah: when Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) freed her, she lost her eyesight. The Quraysh said: "It was none but al-Lat and al-'Uzza who took away her sight." She replied to this: "They are lying; by the House of Allah, al-Lat and al-'Uzza can neither harm nor benefit." After that Allah restored her sight. Nahdiyah and her daughter: both were slave-girls of a woman of the Banu 'Abd al-Dar. She sent them out with flour and said, "By Allah, I will never free you." At that moment Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) was passing by. He said: "O so-and-so, discharge the expiation for this oath and be free of it." She replied: "You pay its expiation; it is you who have spoiled them, so you yourself should free them." He said: "Tell me the price." She said: "This is the price." Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) said: "Very well, I have bought them, and they are free." He said: "Return her flour to her." They said: "It is not proper that we finish with it and then return it." He said: "As you wish."

Likewise, once he passed by a slave-girl who belonged to the Banu Mu'ammal, a branch of the tribe of Banu 'Adi, and was a Muslim. 'Amr ibn Muhayyib used to punish her severely and tell her to abandon Islam; at that time Hadrat 'Umar (رضي الله عنه) was a polytheist, and he was beating her. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 90, verse 16:

"Or feeding on a day of hunger (14:90 to 16) an orphan near of kin, or a needy man lying in the dust." Masghaba means hunger. In days of famine, since food becomes expensive, feeding the poor on such days becomes the criterion for faith.

In the jahili society of that time, the condition of orphans was that their rights were trampled everywhere; their property was embezzled and was swallowed up in such a way that it was as if the earth had consumed it, even when the orphan was a close relative. This is because in that jahili society people were going after wealth like dogs. For this reason the Qur'an had to repeatedly enjoin the protection of the orphan's property, because in that society orphans were subjected to general oppression. Therefore these instructions continued in the Qur'an and were given in the Madani surahs, for example within the laws of inheritance, bequest and marriage. We have discussed this subject in detail in Surah al-Baqarah and Surah al-Nisa.

"Feeding a needy man lying in the dust."

"Or a needy man, full of dust (16:90)." It has been said that, because of his destitution, he is covered in dust. Here, before feeding orphans and the needy, a condition has been placed.

"Feeding an orphan or a needy man on a day of hunger (14:90)." This is because this path has been called the difficult path, and this path is the standard for faith-consciousness, compassion, self-sacrifice and the system of mutual support (takaful) of the Islamic society. People are the family of Allah, and taking care of Allah's dependents is a requirement of faith, especially in days of famine and hunger. And both acts, freeing slaves and feeding the poor, were extremely important in the society of Makkah. Although both these acts are also included in the general objectives of Islam, this is why Allah mentioned them before faith, although believing is a fundamental principle. After this, the general and fundamental principle was mentioned again.

Then he becomes one of those who believe and who enjoin upon one another patience and enjoin upon one another compassion (90:17). ? ? The greatest matter is that a person be among those who believe and who enjoin upon one another patience and compassion.

The word "thumma" (then) here does not carry the sense of "then" in sequence, meaning that first these two deeds come and afterwards Islam; rather, the meaning is that these two partial deeds are also necessary, but faith must come before them. This is a necessary and general principle, and a lofty rank and station. If there is no faith, then freeing slaves and feeding people is not even beneficial. Faith is necessary before every good deed. Weight in any righteous deed before Allah arises solely because of faith, for it is faith that strings deeds together on a consistent, continuous path. Through faith, a righteous deed takes on a continuous and lasting character, whereas without faith, if someone does a good deed, it is merely a temporary enthusiasm, which changes with shifting moods, or a good deed done out of some expediency, or to hear praise.

Now the meaning is this: the difficult ascent is to free a slave, or to feed an orphan or a needy person on a day of hunger, but above all, that he be among the people of faith and among those who counsel one another to patience and compassion. The word "thumma" here, as it were, gives the sense not of "then" but of "the greatest matter is that".

The enjoining of patience is necessary because among the requirements of faith, patience is generally the most important requirement, and to cross a difficult ascent especially requires patience. Then, enjoining one another to patience is a rank higher than patience itself. That is, the Islamic community stands at a level where its members and workers counsel one another to patience, and thus they help one another in fulfilling the requirements of faith, because their feelings are in harmony with one another and they walk together step by step, and they understand that the duty of establishing the system of faith on earth can be discharged only through patience and mutual steadfastness. Therefore, they enjoin one another to patience in the face of the difficulties that arise in the course of this burden, and they become a cause of steadfastness for one another. They give one another encouragement and give one another strength. This mutual patience and mutual enjoining of patience is a higher rank beyond individual patience. Although this patience too rests upon individual patience, the expression "mutual enjoining of patience" indicates that believers should practise collective patience, and that they should not become a cause of breaking one another's resolve but a cause of strengthening it; not a cause of defeat but a cause of advance and of overcoming difficulties; not a cause of lamentation and wailing but a cause of one another's tranquillity.

Likewise, showing mercy to the creatures of God is one matter, and enjoining one another to show mercy to people is a different act, which is an additional matter beyond enjoining mercy. And in this there is an indication that this quality belongs to the community of Muslims: that they counsel one another to mercy, urge one another to act upon it, and regard it as both an individual and a collective duty, so that it becomes the emblem of the members of the community and a point of cooperation.

From patience and mutual enjoining of patience, and from mercy and mutual enjoining of mercy, there emerges the guidance that Islam is a collective religion, for whose establishment a community is necessary, because this is the religion of a community and a society, and through its establishment a nation comes into being. But it is not a collective religion in such a way that individual responsibility is absent from it; rather, it is, as it were, a collective religion founded upon individual responsibility. Individual responsibility is very clear in it.

This is the Urdu commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran) on Surah 90, verse 18. These people who cross that difficult steep path, as the Holy Quran has said:

﴿Those are the companions of the right hand.﴾ (90:18). They are also called Ashab al-Yamin (the companions of the right hand) in another place. These are the people of the right hand and the attribute of felicity and blessedness. Both meanings are bound up with the concept of faith.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 90, verses 19–20:

ʿAlā... [translation begins mid-argument]

The other attributes of the people of the left hand have been omitted from the description.

"And those who rejected Our signs" (90:19). Because when they became disbelievers, the matter was finished. No good deed can be combined with disbelief, nor is any single evil taken into separate account, because every evil lies within disbelief, and disbelief covers it. Therefore there is no need to mention that these people do not free slaves and do not feed the needy. Then, when they rejected the signs of Allah and became disbelievers, no good deed is of any benefit to them at all.

These are the people of the left hand, or the wretched people; both meanings may be intended. They are people of the left hand and also ill-omened, and these same two meanings, namely the right side and the righteous-fortunate in the sense of faith, are also combined. This is because these people did not courageously undertake to cross the difficult steep path.

"Upon them is a fire vaulted over" (90:20). That is, the doors of the Fire are closed upon them, in the literal sense that they have been shut inside and the doors of Hell have been closed over them; or in the sense that the punishment of the Fire has enveloped them. It necessarily means that they will not be able to get out of it. When they cannot remove the fire, it is closed upon them. These two meanings are inseparable.

These fundamental truths, which are the basic matters of human life and the foundations of the creed of faith, have all been compressed into this short surah of a few lines, and have been stated with great clarity and forceful expression. This is the distinctive feature of the Qur'an's manner of expression.

"And those who rejected Our signs" (90:19). Because when they became disbelievers, the matter was finished. No good deed can be combined with disbelief, nor is any single evil taken into separate account, because every evil lies within disbelief, and disbelief covers it. Therefore there is no need to mention that these people do not free slaves and do not feed the needy. Then, when they rejected the signs of Allah and became disbelievers, no good deed is of any benefit to them at all.

These are the people of the left hand, or the wretched people; both meanings may be intended. They are people of the left hand and also ill-omened, and these same two meanings, namely the right side and the righteous-fortunate in the sense of faith, are also combined. This is because these people did not courageously undertake to cross the difficult steep path.

"Upon them is a fire vaulted over" (90:20). That is, the doors of the Fire are closed upon them, in the literal sense that they have been shut inside and the doors of Hell have been closed over them; or in the sense that the punishment of the Fire has enveloped them. It necessarily means that they will not be able to get out of it. When they cannot remove the fire, it is closed upon them. These two meanings are inseparable.

These fundamental truths, which are the basic matters of human life and the foundations of the creed of faith, have all been compressed into this short surah of a few lines, and have been stated with great clarity and forceful expression. This is the distinctive feature of the Qur'an's manner of expression.
